strengths: The paper initiates the parameterized complexity analysis of Satisfiability in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, a natural and well-motivated question given that all classical fragments of the expressivity matrix are NP- or ∃R-hard. The resulting complexity map (Figure 1) is a clear and useful contribution.

Theorem 5's technique is elegant and genuinely distinct from standard treewidth methodology: rather than dynamic programming, the authors construct an LP over bag-marginals whose feasibility is equivalent to the existence of a well-structured SCM. The forward and backward constructions (induction over a BFS traversal of the nice tree decomposition) are carefully argued, and Example 6 makes the construction concrete and easy to follow.

The hardness results are carefully targeted: Theorems 1, 2, 7, 8 and 9 establish intractability under very restrictive conditions (edgeless primal graphs, d=2, maximum degree 8, vertex-disjoint paths of length 2, n=1), which is exactly what is needed to show the tractability results cannot be extended along any of the natural parameter axes. The reductions from 3-SAT, k-Multicolored-Clique, and ETR are appropriate and mostly check out.

The paper is honest about its definitional deviation (sets of inequalities rather than arbitrary Boolean combinations) and explicitly justifies the restriction via Theorem 1, and it clearly delineates what happens with marginalization operators. The writing and motivating examples (diabetes/vaccination/medication) are accessible to a general ICML audience.
The lower-bound technique of Lemma 10 (canonical well-structured models with a single hidden variable encoding function profiles) is a clean structural insight that may be of independent interest.
weaknesses: There appears to be a serious counting error in Theorem 11, one of the two main algorithmic results. Lemma 10 defines Q_i as the set of ALL functions from D^{i-1} to D, whose cardinality is d^{d^{i-1}}, not d^{i-1}·d as claimed in Theorem 11 ('|Q_i| ≤ d^{i−1} · d'). Consequently |Q_1 × ... × Q_n| = d^{Θ(d^n)}, not d^{O(n²)}: the LP has doubly-exponentially (in n) many variables. This invalidates the claimed runtime d^{O(n²)}, and with it Result (5) ('in XP w.r.t. n alone'), since d^{Θ(d^n)} cannot be bounded by |I|^{f(n)} when d is as large as |I|. The claimed EXPTIME inclusion for the marginalization setting (Section 'Extensions to Marginalization') also relies on the incorrect bound. While FPT membership w.r.t. d+n survives (d^{Θ(d^n)} is a computable function of the combined parameter), the advertised bound—and hence Result (5) and parts of Figure 1—are unsupported as stated.

Because of the previous issue, the claimed dichotomy between the prob layer (Theorem 5: XP by treewidth alone) and the causal/counterfactual layers (Theorem 11: XP by n alone) is not established by the presented proof; the distinction that motivates the second set of contributions rests on a bound that does not hold. The authors need to either correct the analysis (possibly yielding a different complexity classification) or provide a genuinely different XP algorithm.

Membership in NP for the restricted SAT*⊛ problems is asserted by citing [13] for arbSAT, but the models considered here may have function representations (case distinctions over hidden variables) of super-polynomial size; the witness-size issue for the restricted problems deserves an explicit argument rather than a citation for a different problem variant.

The gap between the claimed and actual parameter dependence in Theorem 11 (d^{O(n²)} vs. d^{Θ(d^n)}) suggests the algorithmic results may be of limited practical relevance even where correct, and the paper does not discuss the (potentially very large) constants hidden in the FPT bounds or any experimental/empirical validation of the LP-based approaches.

The claim that the technique is 'entirely novel' and incompatible with dynamic programming is asserted rather than precisely substantiated; the LP-over-bag-marginals idea is close in spirit to consistency-based formulations of joins over tree decompositions, and a more careful comparison to related decomposition-based LP/ILP techniques would strengthen the novelty claim.

strengths: The paper initiates the parameterized complexity analysis of Satisfiability in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, a natural and previously unmapped question given that all classical fragments are NP- or ∃R-hard. The identified 'gateways' (FPT for SAT^lin_prob by d+tw, XP by tw; FPT for SAT^lin_counterfact by d+n, XP by n) are clearly stated and complemented by lower bounds (W[1]-hardness by n, NP-hardness for d=2 with edgeless/bounded-degree or path-structured primal graphs, ∃R-hardness for the poly fragment even with n=1 or d=2 and edgeless graphs), yielding a fairly complete picture of where tractability ends.

The algorithmic technique is a genuine departure from the standard dynamic programming over tree decompositions: a global LP over bag-assignment probabilities with consistency constraints, plus a constructive argument (Theorem 5's BFS construction and Lemma 10's well-structured models) that any LP solution corresponds to an actual SCM. This is a clean and potentially reusable idea for problems mixing discrete structure with continuous/probabilistic components.

The manuscript is technically careful and self-contained: definitions of syntax, semantics, SCMs, and treewidth are precise; all theorems come with full proofs; the worked example (Example 6) substantially aids readability of the LP construction. The treatment of the restricted setting (sets of inequalities rather than Boolean combinations) is honest — the authors flag the deviation from prior work and prove (Theorem 1) that the unrestricted variant remains NP-hard even on edgeless graphs with d=2, justifying the restriction rather than hiding it.

The extension discussion on marginalization operators (bounding nesting depth of Σ, EXPTIME vs. NEXP separation) and the Observation 4 domain-reduction are useful and show awareness of the limits of the approach.
weaknesses: The claimed novelty of the technique is overstated. Constructing an LP whose variables represent joint assignments over bags of a tree decomposition, with marginalization-consistency constraints between adjacent bags, is essentially the classical junction-tree/cluster-tree LP formulation (exactness of local consistency on trees is a well-known fact underlying junction-tree propagation and LP relaxations of marginal polytopes). The derivation of an SCM from such an LP is a nice adaptation, but presenting the approach as 'entirely novel' overstates the delta relative to known decompositional LP methods.

The contribution's practical significance is limited. The FPT algorithm runs in d^{f(tw)}|ϕ|^{O(1)} and the counterfactual algorithm in n!·(|ϕ|^{O(1)}+d^{O(n^2)}); both are purely theoretical, and the tractable fragments are restrictive (linear inequalities, no Boolean combinations, no marginalization). The paper offers no evidence — empirical or via use cases — that these gateways matter for instances arising in practice.

The phrase 'matching hardness results' is not strictly accurate. The lower bounds rule out specific parameterizations (no FPT by tw alone, no FPT by n alone, no XP by d alone, no lifting to poly), but they do not match the upper bounds in a tight sense; e.g., whether the XP-by-tw classification for SAT^lin_prob is optimal is left open. The lower-bound reductions (from 3-SAT, k-Multicolored-Clique, and a restricted ETR variant) are competent but largely standard, with Theorem 8's reduction in particular being quite routine.

Fit and significance for the ICML audience are debatable: the paper is a pure complexity-theory contribution with no learning content, and the causal-reasoning community results it builds on ([13, 32, 45, 9]) are mostly published at IJCAI/ICLR/LP venues. The main audience appears to be parameterized-complexity/AI-theory rather than machine learning.

Some results are easy consequences of others and the framing as eight bullet 'results' inflates the contribution: e.g., (4) and (8) are hardness transfers of (3)/(7) type arguments, and the XP-by-tw claim follows from the FPT-by-d+tw algorithm plus d ≤ |ϕ|+1.

strengths: The paper provides the first systematic parameterized-complexity treatment of satisfiability in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, and the results form a complete, tight picture: XP/FPT upper bounds (Theorems 5 and 11) are matched by lower bounds under the same parameterizations (Theorems 7, 8, 9), giving a definitive classification rather than isolated results.

The hardness results are established under very restrictive settings (e.g., NP-hardness for SAT^lin_causal even with d=2 and G_phi consisting of vertex-disjoint length-2 paths in Theorem 9; NP-hardness for SAT^base_prob with d=2 and max degree 8 in Theorem 7), which makes the negative results strong and informative for charting the tractability frontier in Figure 1.

The paper handles the deviation from prior work (sets of inequalities vs. arbitrary Boolean combinations) carefully: Theorem 1 shows that allowing Boolean combinations destroys all hope of exploiting structure (NP-complete even with edgeless G_phi and d=2), which cleanly justifies the problem definition.

The structural insights are genuinely interesting: Lemma 10 (existence of 'well-structured' SCMs in which a single hidden variable encodes the entire function profile) is a clean and potentially reusable normal-form result, and the LP-based constructions avoid exponential blowup in input size, which is the technically delicate part.

The manuscript is largely self-contained (syntax, semantics, treewidth, ∃R all defined), includes a worked example (Example 6) illustrating the LP construction, and all proofs are included, supporting reproducibility for a theory contribution. The marginalization extension (Section 'Extensions to Marginalization') is honestly and precisely delineated, including the EXPTIME vs NEXP barrier for full summation operators.
weaknesses: The claimed technical novelty is overstated. The introduction and concluding remarks advertise the treewidth-based approach as 'entirely novel' and assert that dynamic programming is 'entirely incompatible' with the problem. However, the LP over bag-distributions with pairwise marginal-consistency constraints in Theorem 5 is essentially the classical junction-tree/cluster LP technique long used in probabilistic reasoning and probabilistic satisfiability (Nilsson 1986; Georgakopoulos et al. 1988 — both cited only as 'related languages'). The contribution is better described as adapting a known LP technique to a new problem; the framing should be tempered.

Theorem 11's XP/FPT algorithm is comparatively straightforward: it enumerates all n! variable orderings and, per ordering, solves an LP over d^{O(n^2)} function profiles. The interest rests almost entirely on Lemma 10; the algorithmic step itself is close to brute force, and the runtime n!·(|phi|^{O(1)} + d^{O(n^2)}) is unlikely to be practically meaningful.

Significance is somewhat specialized. The positive results cover only the lin fragments (SAT^lin_prob, SAT^lin_counterfact); the poly layer is ∃R-hard even in extremely restricted forms (Theorem 2), and full marginalization is ruled out by NEXP-completeness. Thus the 'gateways to tractability' occupy a fairly narrow region of the expressivity matrix, and the practical impact on the ML/AI audience of ICML is limited — there are no experiments or algorithmic refinements (e.g., improved FPT dependence) that would make the results actionable.

Some proofs are compressed to the point where the reader must reconstruct nontrivial steps. For example, the reverse direction of Theorem 9 asserts 'there is j such that L_j does not precede its counterpart and thus ℓ_i is set to TRUE' without spelling out why a positive-probability summand forces the ordering condition; Observation 4's proof relies on an unproven 'without loss of generality' about case-distinction representations of the functions. These steps appear correct but deserve full arguments.

Minor presentation issues: unusual phrasing ('a contingent of random variables'), models written as (V, ∅, F, ∅) with an empty probability distribution (slightly awkward; a trivial single-point exogenous variable would be cleaner), and the discussion of why DP is impossible is rhetorical rather than backed by a formal impossibility argument.

strengths: The paper delivers an essentially complete and tight parameterized complexity classification of Satisfiability across the 3x3 expressivity matrix of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, combining new FPT/XP algorithms (Theorems 5 and 11) with matching conditional lower bounds (Theorems 7, 8, 9, and strengthened hardness for the poly fragment in Theorem 2), leaving only a clearly stated open question (XP vs. polytime for SATlin_counterfact parameterized by n).

The algorithmic technique is genuinely interesting and departs from the standard dynamic programming paradigm for treewidth: for SATlin_prob, the authors first show every YES-instance admits a well-structured SCM whose hidden variables align with a nice tree decomposition, and then verify existence via a fixed-parameter-sized linear program (Theorem 5). This 'treewidth-guided linear programming' is a novel toolkit with plausible further applications, and is argued convincingly with an instructive worked example (Example 6).

The results are well-motivated: prior work (Fagin et al., Mossé et al., van der Zander et al.) showed NP- or ∃R-hardness for even the easiest fragments, so the identification of the first tractability islands, together with careful demarcation of where tractability breaks (e.g., NP-hardness already at treewidth 1 for SATlin_causal, Theorem 9), is a significant contribution to the understanding of causal reasoning complexity.

Hardness results are appropriately strengthened to very restricted settings (edgeless primal graphs, d = 2, single variable, bounded degree, vertex-disjoint edges), which makes the lower bounds robust and directly rules out the relevant parameterized tractability notions; the ∃R-hardness restriction (Theorem 2) goes beyond the previously known statement of Mossé et al.

The paper is clearly written, honest about deviations from prior problem definitions (sets of inequalities vs. Boolean combinations, justified via Theorem 1), and explicitly discusses extensions to marginalization operators, including why full marginalization provably cannot be handled (EXPTIME vs. NEXP-complete), plus an open problems section with substantive future directions.
weaknesses: The contribution is purely theoretical with no implementation or empirical evaluation; the FPT algorithm of Theorem 11 runs in n! · d^{O(d^n)} time (enumerating all n! variable orders and solving LPs of size d^{O(d^n)}), and even the more practical Theorem 5 algorithm has a d^{O(tw)} LP, so the practical relevance of the 'gateways to tractability' for realistic instances remains untested.

The claim that the technique is 'entirely novel' is somewhat overstated: LP formulations over bag assignments combined with tree decompositions are reminiscent of known approaches (e.g., LP-based probabilistic satisfiability à la Nilsson/Georgakopoulos et al. combined with structural decompositions); the novelty lies mainly in the two-step structure (well-structured SCM existence + LP verification) rather than in a fundamentally new machinery.

Several minor presentation issues: in the Proof Techniques section (page 5), the counterfactual structural result is mis-referenced as 'Result (5)' instead of Lemma 10/Theorem 11; typos such as 'the ϕ is satisfied' (Lemma 10), 'U′F′' (Example 6), and inconsistent naming of Theorem 3 vs. Observation 3 in Theorem 11's proof slightly detract from polish.

The FPT result for SATlin_counterfact (Theorem 11) relies on Lemma 10's normal form with a single hidden variable of domain Q1 × ... × Qn; while the proof is correct, the classification leaves a somewhat unsatisfying asymmetry between the shallow fragment (parameterized by treewidth + d) and the deep fragments (parameterized by n + d), and the paper does not attempt intermediate parameterizations (e.g., treewidth + d + restricted structure for causal/counterfactual fragments) beyond the hardness of Theorem 9.

The lower bounds are conditional on standard assumptions (P ≠ NP, FPT ≠ W[1], ∃R not in FPT) rather than unconditional, which is appropriate for the field but means the 'tightness' claims are assumption-dependent; this is disclosed but could be more prominently flagged in the abstract.

strengths: The paper delivers the first systematic parameterized complexity analysis of Satisfiability in Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, and the classification is essentially tight: positive results (FPT for SATprob_lin by d+tw, XP by tw, FPT for SATcounterfact_lin by d+n; Theorems 5 and 11) are paired with matching lower bounds under standard assumptions (Theorems 2, 7, 8, 9), giving a nearly complete map of the 3x3 expressivity matrix from the parameterized viewpoint.

The hardness results are established under remarkably strong restrictions, which strengthens them considerably: Theorem 1 shows NP-completeness of arbSAT with edgeless primal graphs and d=2, Theorem 2 shows ∃R-completeness even for n=1 or edgeless binary instances, and Theorem 9 shows NP-completeness of SATcausal_lin even when all edges of the primal graph are pairwise vertex-disjoint. These restrictions genuinely 'rule out tractability in the parameterized setting' as claimed.

The positive results avoid the standard leaf-to-root dynamic programming paradigm, which the authors convincingly argue is incompatible with the problem. The two-step approach (structural normalization of the SCM followed by a fixed-parameter sized LP, Theorem 5; the 'single hidden variable determines the structural function' construction in Lemma 10 for Theorem 11) is a genuinely different technique for treewidth-based tractability and could plausibly find further applications, as the authors suggest.

The treatment of definitions is careful and honest: the deviation from prior SAT* definitions (sets of inequalities rather than arbitrary Boolean combinations) is explicitly flagged and justified via Theorem 1; the extension to marginalization operators is honestly bounded (EXPTIME membership vs. NEXP-completeness, so no lift), and the constant-nesting-depth workaround is correctly identified.

Proofs are written out in full in the main text, including a worked example (Example 6) tracing the LP construction and the corresponding model; this aids verification and reproducibility of the mathematical arguments.
weaknesses: The practical significance of the 'gateways to tractability' is limited. The FPT algorithm of Theorem 5 runs in d^f(tw)*|ϕ|^O(1), and Theorem 11 runs in n!*(|ϕ|^O(1) + d^O(d^n)), which involves a double-exponential dependence on n in the exponent. Even the LP in Theorem 11 has up to d^(d^n) variables. For realistic causal models these running times are astronomically large, so the contribution is almost purely complexity-theoretic; the paper would benefit from a franker discussion of the gap between parameterized tractability and practical applicability.

The claim that the treewidth-based technique (Results 1 and 2) is 'entirely novel' is somewhat overstated. The core of Theorem 5—representing a consistent joint distribution via an LP over bags of a tree decomposition with marginalization consistency constraints—is structurally close to classical junction-tree/cluster-based consistency formulations and to LP-based approaches to probabilistic satisfiability going back to Nilsson [32] and Georgakopoulos et al. [20]; the novelty lies mainly in the reverse direction of the proof (constructing an SCM from an LP solution via chained hidden variables) rather than in the LP formulation itself.

The parameterization by d + n for the deeper layers (Result 5) feels weak: the algorithm enumerates all n! variable orders and the hardness results (Theorems 7-9) show that neither parameter alone suffices, so the gateway is narrow. The paper itself concedes the open question of even an XP algorithm for SATcounterfact_lin parameterized by n alone, which indicates the classification is less complete than the framing 'almost complete picture' suggests.

There is an asymmetry in the lower-bound strength: Results (3) and (6) are supported by W[1]-hardness (Theorem 8), but Result (4) for the lin-causal case and Result (5)'s tightness rely on NP-completeness statements (Theorems 9 and 7) whose relationship to FPT/XP in the parameterized sense is only argued indirectly (e.g., tw(ϕ) ≤ n in the discussion after Theorem 8). A cleaner separation of which hardness assumption rules out which algorithmic guarantee would improve rigor of the 'matching' claims.

The restriction to recursive SCMs with a fixed well-order ≺ and to single-variable, finite-domain hidden variables is silently load-bearing in several proofs (e.g., Lemma 10's partition argument and Observation 4's contraction procedure). The paper states the reduction from continuous exogenous domains to finite ones via [46], but does not discuss whether restricting to recursive models (as opposed to general SCMs, e.g., with cyclic or simultaneous structure) matches the definitions used in the works from which the hardness baselines are imported.

The paper contains no empirical component whatsoever—no implementation, no experiments, not even a discussion of whether the LP-based algorithms could be implemented and scaled on small instances. For a theory paper this is acceptable, but combined with the enormous running times it makes the contribution relevant to a rather specialized audience even within the ICML community.

Minor presentation issues: the running-time claim in Theorem 5's proof (d^f(tw)|ϕ|^O(1)) is stated with an unspecified f and the XP/FPT dichotomy within the single algorithm is left implicit; the proof of Theorem 5 implicitly assumes connectivity handling for disconnected primal graphs is routine without spelling it out; and the phrase 'dashing any hope' is informal for a paper of this register.

strengths: First systematic parameterized complexity analysis of Satisfiability across Pearl's Causal Hierarchy, filling a genuine gap: prior work (Fagin et al.; Mossé et al.; van der Zander et al.; Dörfler et al.) established only NP- and ∃R-completeness, leaving structural tractability unexplored.

The results are complete and tight: for each tractability claim there is a matching conditional lower bound (Theorems 2, 7, 8, 9 establish hardness under strong restrictions such as d=2, edgeless primal graphs, n=1, or pairwise vertex-disjoint edges), giving a definitive map of the tractability landscape for the lin/base fragments.

The main algorithmic contribution (Theorem 5) is conceptually interesting: rather than the standard leaf-to-root dynamic programming over tree decompositions, the authors reduce to a polynomial-size LP whose variables represent bag-distributions with pairwise consistency constraints, and then construct a witness SCM from an LP solution. The correctness argument (induction over a BFS traversal of the decomposition) is careful and convincing, and Example 6 substantially aids comprehension.

Theorem 11 (FPT for SAT^lin_counterfact w.r.t. d+n) is a pleasant surprise given that enumeration of models is useless in the causal setting; the supporting Lemma 10 (well-structured single-hidden-variable canonical form) is a clean structural insight.

Well-scoped and honest treatment of limitations: the paper explicitly explains why the restriction to sets of inequalities matters (Theorem 1), why marginalization operators cannot be handled in full (with a precise EXPTIME vs. NEXP-completeness argument), and clearly separates already-known hardness (∃R for the poly fragment) from the new, stronger restricted versions.

Self-contained and clearly written: preliminaries cover syntax, semantics, tree decompositions, and ∃R; all proofs (including hardness reductions from 3-SAT, k-Multicolored-Clique, and ETR) are included and appear correct on a careful read.
weaknesses: The claim that the technique is an 'entirely novel approach' is somewhat oversold. The LP over bags with pairwise consistency constraints closely resembles cluster/tree-based LP relaxations and local-consistency formulations known from probabilistic inference and CSP (e.g., junction-tree consistency LPs, Samer–Szeider-style structural approaches). The paper would benefit from a more precise positioning of what exactly is new relative to these known LP-over-decomposition ideas.

The paper is purely theoretical with no implementation or experiments; the practical relevance of, e.g., the d^{f(tw)} dependence in Theorem 5 or the n!·d^{O(d^n)} bound in Theorem 11 is questionable for typical AI workloads, and the manuscript does not discuss when these parameters are small in practice.

Some rough edges in presentation: occasional typos (e.g., '(V, U′F′, ℙ′)' in Example 6, the marginalization operator Σ rendered inconsistently), and Theorem 9's reverse-direction argument compresses the case analysis on the well-order into a few lines that a reader must reconstruct (in particular, why a fractional LP-style sum ≥ 1 cannot be witnessed by literal probabilities that are inconsistent with the derived assignment α).

The discussion of why W[1]-hardness w.r.t. n implies no FPT w.r.t. treewidth alone is correct but terse; given that treewidth ≤ n, a sentence making the monotonicity argument explicit (as done for Theorem 7) would help.

Fit to the ICML audience is a consideration: the contribution is a complexity-theoretic classification with no learning component; readers seeking algorithmic causal-inference tools will find the algorithms mostly of theoretical interest. This is a scope rather than quality concern.

Minor: the necessity of restricting to sets of inequalities (arbSAT vs. SAT) is handled well for hardness, but the interaction of this restriction with the XP/FPT algorithms (e.g., whether Boolean combinations beyond sets could be handled with comparable running times) is not discussed.
